title: Right to an Interpreter
statement: the court must give you a qualified interpreter for your hearings
source_name: Evidence Code 756; California Courts Self-Help Guide, Ask for an interpreter
source_says: If sufficient funds are not appropriated to provide an interpreter to every party
steps: Searched 'Evidence Code 756 interpreter', opened public.law section 756 and the selfhelp.courts.ca.gov page. Section 756 says reimbursement is 'To the extent required by other state or federal laws' and sets a priority order when funds are short; it does not use 'must' or 'qualified'. Self-help page says interpreters 'are provided free of charge' and that you 'must request an interpreter in advance'. The dependency booklet (p. 6) only says to tell the judge you need one.
fix: The court gives you an interpreter for your hearings at no cost. You have to ask for one, so ask as early as you can.

title: Right to Be Present at Hearings
statement: You have the right to attend every hearing in your case.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court rule 5.530(b); WIC 349(a); WIC 290.1(b); Judicial Council booklet p. 3
source_says: All parents, de facto parents, Indian custodians, and guardians of the child
steps: Opened WIC 349 (persons entitled to notice under 290.1, 290.2, 291, 293, 294 are 'entitled to be present'), rule 5.530(b) ('The following persons are entitled to be present'), and WIC 290.1/291, which say no notice is required for a parent whose parental rights have been terminated. Booklet p. 3 says 'Go to and participate in all court hearings about your children, unless your parental rights were ended.' The entry leaves that condition out.
fix: You have the right to go to the hearings in your case, unless your parental rights have been ended.

title: Right to Be Present at Hearings
statement: At each hearing, the judge will advise you of your rights and what is happening.
source_name: Cal. Rules of Court rule 5.534(c) and (g)
source_says: At each hearing, the court must advise any self-represented child, parent, or guardian of the right to be represented by counsel
steps: Opened rule 5.534 on courts.ca.gov. Subdivision (g)(1) says 'The court must advise the child, parent, and guardian in section 300 cases' of hearing rights but states no timing. Only (c), on the right to a lawyer for people without one, says 'At each hearing'.
fix: The judge must tell you about your hearing rights. If you do not have a lawyer, the judge must tell you at each hearing that you can have one.

title: Right to Be Present at Hearings
statement: If you cannot physically attend, ask your attorney about appearing by phone or video.

steps: Searched 'rule 3.672 remote juvenile dependency', opened courts.ca.gov rule 3.672, read subdivision (i): such a person may request to appear remotely (form RA-025), and remote technology covers video and audio or audio alone. The court can still require in-person appearance in listed situations.

title: Right to a Say About Medication
statement: You cannot be given medication unless it is prescribed for you or it is an emergency.
source_name: WIC 16001.9(a)(23); CA Foster Care Ombudsperson, Foster Youth Bill of Rights Handbook p. 25
source_says: Except in an emergency, to be free of the administration of medication or chemical substances,
steps: Searched 'Welfare and Institutions Code 16001.9 foster youth rights california.public.law', opened the public.law page (says updated Jan. 1, 2026) through the fetch tool, which returned the paragraph word for word in short segments. Read (a)(23): the emergency exception is there, but the words 'unless prescribed by a physician' are attached to psychotropic medications, not to all medication. Then searched for the Ombudsperson youth rights handbook, opened the 2026 FYBOR Handbook PDF on fosteryouthhelp.ca.gov; p. 25 says 'Yes. You can refuse any medication, vitamin, or herb.' and 'No one can give you consequences or punish you for refusing.' Neither source says a prescription is what allows medication to be given. Paragraph number (23) in Anchor's legal_reference matches the current text.
fix: You can say no to medication, except in an emergency. No one can punish you for saying no. Talk to your doctor about the risks first.

title: Right to a Say About Medication
statement: Medication for mental health needs a doctor's prescription and a judge's approval.
source_says: to be free of all psychotropic medications unless prescribed by a physician, and in the case of children, authorized by a judge, without consequences or retaliation.
steps: Searched 'Welfare and Institutions Code 16001.9 foster youth rights california.public.law', opened the public.law page (says updated Jan. 1, 2026) through the fetch tool, which returned the paragraph word for word in short segments. Read (a)(23): judge approval is 'in the case of children'. Also opened public.law WIC 369.5 (https://california.public.law/codes/ca_welf_and_inst_code_section_369.5): 'only a juvenile court judicial officer shall have authority to make orders regarding the administration of psychotropic medications for that child' and the court may delegate this to a parent. The Ombudsperson handbook p. 26 says 'A judge has to approve any psychotropic medications a doctor prescribes.' with no age condition, and also 'You have the right to refuse psychotropic medication'.
fix: Medication for mental health needs a doctor's prescription. If you are under 18, a judge must also approve it. You can say no to it, and no one can punish you for that.

title: Right to Reunification Services
statement: Even if the agency tries to skip services due to past issues, you have the right to argue why services would benefit your child.
source_says: unless the court finds, by clear and convincing evidence, that reunification is in the best interest of the child.
steps: Searched 'Welfare and Institutions Code 361.5 reunification services', opened the public.law page through the fetch tool and had it quote subdivisions (a), (b) and (c) word for word. (c)(1): 'the court shall hold a dispositional hearing.' (c)(2): 'The court shall not order reunification for a parent or guardian described in paragraph (3), (4), (6), (7) ... or (17) of subdivision (b)' unless it makes the finding quoted here. The statute sets a high bar (clear and convincing evidence) and words it as a finding the court may make, not as a named right to argue. Anchor's legal_reference to 361.5 and 361.5(c) points to the right subdivisions.
